newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan parades warplanes to counter rival China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan parades warplanes to counter rival China.

text.p: Taiwan commissioned a third squadron of locally-made warplanes and has taken delivery of its first U.S. F-16 fighters, hailing both as vital to counter rival China's military modernisation.

In a morning of gun salutes and flypasts, Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling said on Tuesday the Indigenous Defence Fighters (IDFs) formed a "modern fighting wing" fully capable of protecting Taiwan against Chinese threats.
Commanders confirmed that Taiwan had taken delivery on Monday of the first two of 150 advanced F-16 fighters ordered from the United States in a deal that outraged Beijing.

"Communist China, from its speeches to the outside world and its internal military buildup, has never changed its chosen route of trying to rely on military weapons to resolve the cross-strait dispute," Chiang said at the gala commissioning at an air base in central Taichung.
"This modern fighting wing absolutely has the capability to defend the skies of the Taiwan strait," he added.

As Taiwan put its new planes through their paces, the commanding officer of China's air force was quoted as saying Beijing would build up state-of-the-art air force weapons systems by early in the next century.
China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since the two split after a civil war in 1949, vows to retake the island eventually, by force of necessary.
Such threats, manifested in war games near the island in 1995 and 1996, have led Taiwan to bolster its defences.
The 24 IDFs commissioned on Tuesday, which carry Taiwan-made Sky Sword air-to-air missiles and other weapons, joined a 70-fighter wing based in the Taiwan Strait city of Taichung.
The ministry said it planned to complete a 60-strong IDF wing by 2000 in Tainan in southern Taiwan.
The IDFs, along with the 150 U.S. F-16s and 60 Mirages bought from France, were expected to become the mainstay of Taiwan's air defences against China.
The Defence Ministry said the two F-16s delivered on Monday would be reinforced by others through 1997.
"We have successfully taken the first two planes," ministry spokesman Huang Hsien-jung said in Taichung. "The first squadron (of F-16s) should be formed by the end of the year."
The ministry has not said when other F-16 deliveries were expected.

But it has said that France will begin delivering the 60 Mirages in May and that the deal was unaffected by Paris's promise, made under pressure from Beijing following the Mirage sale, to stop arming the island.
Beijing sees sales of advanced foreign military technology to Taiwan as an encroachment on its sovereignty.

Military experts said China's armed forces were far from advanced but that a sustained drive to upgrade its technology and to develop a generation of locally made fighters were key factors prompting Taiwan to order the F-16s.
"This is part of the impetus that has driven Taiwan to substantially advance its own air force," said Robert Karniol, Bangkok-based Asia correspondent for Jane's Defence Weekly.

China has been acquiring Su-27 fighters from Russia, building the Su-27SK air superiority fighter at home under licence from Russia and developing its indigenous F-10 multi-role fighter, military analysts said.

Beijing held war games and missile tests near Taiwan before the island's first direct presidential election in March 1996 in what Beijing acknowledged was a warning to Taiwanese voters not to drop a pledge to reunify with the mainland.
